items.title: Sublime Seixas Becomes Youngest-Ever Winner of IL Lombardia with Huge Solo Move
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Paul Seixas reaffirms huge potential with stomping solo victory, capturing the first Monument success of his career.
items.lbText:
Paul Seixas wins Il Lombardia (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images) (Photo: @DarioBelingheri/@GettyImages)

Paul Seixas further underlined his staggering talent with an assured win at Il Lombardia , taking the first Monument win of his career and becoming the youngest-ever winner.

The 20 year old drove forward with 19.2km to go to drop most of the other big contenders on the Civiglio, the penultimate climb of the day. He went over the top well clear of European championships runner-up Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek) and Tom Pidcock (Pinarello Q36.5 Pro Cycling), with the latter being replaced by Vuelta winner Enric Mas (Movistar)

Seixas powered up the second and final ascent of the San Fermo Della Battaglia, with Mas dropping Ciccone in a bid to close up to him.

However he was far too strong, racing in well clear and savoring the biggest win of his career.

Mas raced in for second place, 48 seconds back, with Ciccone taking third in his final race for his team.

Seixas looked stunned by what he had done, and said that things hadn’t really sunk in by the time he did the post-race interview.

“It is crazy. I think I don’t realize [it] for now,” he said. “Everything went perfect, the team did a great, awesome job. Everyone pushed more than what they had to do.”

His Decathlon CMA CGM team did indeed dedicate themselves to him, helping him to save energy until it most counted.

“I had amazing legs. I had the feeling that today was a great day,” he continued. “I managed to make the difference at the moment I choose. Maybe a bit earlier because I felt like the rhythm was not high enough at the start of the climb, for me at least, to make the difference.

“So I had to accelerate early, maybe a bit too early. There were some not really steep parts, so I had to manage really well my effort and accelerate in the hard parts. I did the best TT I could, me against myself. It was crazy.”

New European champion Remco Evenepoel had to be satisfied with fourth place, something well below his pre-race ambitions. He crashed in Il Lombardia in his 2020 debut, going over the side of a bridge and falling several meters to the ground.

He fractured his pelvis and has tried to win the race several time since. He was second to Tadej Pogačar in 2024 and 2025 and with Pogačar absent due to injury, he felt he might have his big victory this time around.

That optimism was furthered by his victory in the Euros last weekend but, once the pressure was applied, he found himself slipping backwards and losing contact with the other big challengers.

Just as was the case at the worlds, he dangled off the back of the groups his rival were in, but eventually fought his way forward again towards the end. He led the sprint in for fourth place, 1:20 back, with new world champion Brandon McNulty (UAE Emirates-XRG) continuing his stomping end of season with fifth place.

“I think I had bad position going into the penultimate climb,” he said. “I made a bit of an effort to come to the front and went a little deep on the wheel of Paul and paid for it.

“I felt really good today. But then that climb, I went into the red. That was it.”

The final Monument of the season was, as ever, a very tough one. It packed in 4662 vertical meters over 239km, and was enlivened by a big breakaway sparked off 211 kilometers out by Uno-X Mobility rider Johannes Kulse.

Andrea Mifsud (Team Polti VisitMalta), Micahel Leonard, Ben O’Connor (Jayco-AlUla) and Maxime Decomble (Groupama-FDJ United) got across, while Antonio Tiberi (Bahrain Victorious), Sylvain Moniquet (Cofidis), Fausto Masnada (MBH Bank Csb Telecom Fort), George Bennett, Pau Martí (NSN), Gijs Leemreize (Picnic PostNL) and Louis Vervaeke (Soudal Quick-Step) did likewise soon afterwards.

Julien Bernard (Lidl-Trek) and Victor Campenaerts (Visma-Lease a Bike) made it 14 and together they build a lead of almost three minutes.

O’Connor hacked down the break’s size when he set a furious pace on the Ghisallo. Their lead was 1:29 with 61.5km remaining, with the pace heating up behind when Louis Barre (Visma-Lease a Bike) went all out to platform a huge move by Matteo Jorgenson.

The American was joined by compatriots Quinn Simmons (Lidl-Trek) and Brandon McNulty (UAE Emirates-XRG), as well as the Italian Christian Scaroni (XDS Astana).

However Giulio Pellizzari put in a huge effort and brought them back several kilometers later, then continued to plough along at the front for Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe. Simmons had been the fastest up the Ghisallo but had the misfortune to experience a mechanical, ruining his chances.

Pellizzari continued to set a determined pace on the climb of San Fermo Della Battaglia and put Jorgenson, Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), Juan Ayuso (Lidl-Trek) and Lenny Martinez (Bahrain-Victorious) out the back. His efforts ensured the break had just 44 seconds crossing the finish line with 21.8km to go, and while Leonard pushed clear alone soon afterwards on the climb of Civiglio, he was reeled in soon afterwards.

Isaac Del Toro was the big hope for UAE and Adam Yates did most of the work on that climb. However it was Seixas who was strongest. He stomped away with 19.2km remaining, Pidcock and Ciccone clinging on briefly before being forced to slow.

Pidcock’s place in the chase was taken by soon afterwards by Mas, with the Vuelta winner dropping Ciccone on the San Fermo Della Battaglia but having zero success in trying to get back up to Seixas.

The Frenchman was absolutely flying. He may have been the youngest rider in the whole race but he was far above the level of the rest.

“It is a dream. Today my legs made me dream today and then I had an opportunity,” he smiled.

“I really trained hard for this. It is incredible.”

It is, and it set things up for some fascinating clashes with Pogačar next season.

Tom Pidcock (Pinarello Q36.5 Procycling) was sixth, with nine riders in total in this group.

items.title: ‘People Are Dying’: Riders Delay Il Lombardia in Rare Public Protest Over Safety
items.author: ahood
items.content: A frustrated peloton stages a five-minute protest and issues a joint statement demanding tighter course security and action from the UCI and race organizers.
items.lbText:
Remco Evenepoel, shown here with world champion Brandon McNulty, spoke out on behalf of the peloton over rider safety. (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images)

The riders have had enough, and the bunch delayed Il Lombardia for five minutes Saturday morning to demand safer roads after another ugly week of vehicles getting onto race courses .

World champion Brandon McNulty and European champion Remco Evenepoel stood at the front as the peloton held up the season’s final monument to demand rider safety .

Evenepoel grabbed the microphone and spoke for the riders in a rare public showing of solidarity.

“In the name of the whole bunch and not only for the guys that are here but for everybody pro cycling, we want to make this statement because there’s too many incidents happening with vehicles in the race,” Evenepoel said.

“Unfortunately, we lost the life of a brother and of a colleague of us,” he said. “We want to make this statement to just show to the whole world that we cannot keep accepting the fact that guys are getting injured and are literally dying while doing what we like the most.”

The riders and the CPA also issued a joint statement asking the UCI and race organizers to take responsibility and tighten course security ( see statement below ).

Frustration has been bubbling behind the scenes ever since 19-year-old Finlay Tarling was killed following a collision with a vehicle that entered the Volta a Portugal course in August.

Michael Tarling, the father of Finlay, took to X to support the solidarity among the riders.

“We are so thankful, moved and proud of Fin’s fellow cyclists today for making a stand at the Tour of Lombardy,” he wrote. “Things need to change and no other family should ever receive the phone call we received on 14th Aug. We sincerely hope the UCI are listening and changes will be made.”

‼️ La protesta del pelotón, encabezada por Remco Evenepoel, antes del inicio de #IlLombardia ⚠️ El movimiento llega tras los últimos incidentes con vehículos de carrera estas semanas #LaCasadelCiclismo pic.twitter.com/OgEwYGlIwq

Saturday’s protest comes on the heels of high-profile vehicle incidents at both Coppa Bernocchi and Tre Valli Varesine this week in Italy.

At Monday’s Coppa Bernocchi, a DHL delivery van pulled onto the route from a side street and drove behind the breakaway before stopping.

A day later, a police motorbike traveling against the direction of racing collided with Tom Pidcock’s Pinarello-Q36.5 teammates Thomas Gloag and Marcel Camprubí at Tre Valli Varesine.

Gloag abandoned and required stitches to his knee , while Camprubí continued and later complained that “nothing changes.”

Heavy crashes have marked racing this week in Italy as well .

The latest incidents add to a grim toll the past few years. Gino Mäder died after crashing at the 2023 Tour de Suisse, André Drege died while descending at the Tour of Austria in 2024, and junior racer Muriel Furrer died following a crash at the 2024 UCI Road World Championships.

“This is why we want to stand for five minutes more, to make our statement towards organizations, to the public, to everybody that is following cycling and accepting the fact that people are dying,” Evenepoel said.

The UCI has introduced new safety measures , including better barriers and signage, but riders want faster action and stronger protection on race roads.

“We want to pay our tribute and respect to everybody that was already involved in the incidents,” he said.

After the protest, the race started without further incident.

There was no immediate response from the UCI.

As riders, we stand united against the unnecessary risk our lives are being subjected to.

This week alone, there were multiple incidents of vehicles on race courses. Two riders crashed when they hit a motorbike who was driving the wrong way on the race route. Luckily both escaped with cuts and bruises, it could have been so much worse.

This summer, a life was tragically lost to exactly this kind of failure. We will not stand for this any longer.

Riders race at high speed with little protection, and we depend on the race organisers to secure the roads. That responsibility is not being met.

We are calling for the help of the UCI for race organisers to take accountability and act. That means a serious, open conversation between riders, race organisers and the UCI resulting in concrete changes to how race routes are secured and managed.

After five minutes, we raced as normal. We did not want to affect the race, only to show what riders can do when we stand as one.

We love this sport. We respect the race organisers. We want to race hard and put on a show for our fans. However most importantly we want to come home safe to our loved ones.

items.title: Marianne Vos Wins UCI Gravel Worlds, Gomez Villafañe Sixth, Heavy Crash Mars Race
items.author: ahood
items.content: Results: Vos claims her second gravel world title at thrilling first edition outside Europe, Geerike Schreurs involved in a heavy crash.
items.lbText:
Vos, pictured here in the 2024 edition, won her second UCI gravel worlds title in a wild race Saturday. (Photo: JASPER JACOBS / BELGA MAG / Belga via AFP)

Marianne Vos claimed a second UCI Gravel World Championship title Saturday in Nannup, Australia, winning solo after a showdown with Rosa Klöser as U.S.-based gravel star Sofia Gomez Villafañe finished sixth.

A heavy crash involving Geerike Schreurs and Ashleigh Moolman-Pasio overshadowed the race.

“This victory really means a lot to me,” Vos said.

Germany’s Klöser finished 27 seconds behind Vos after slipping out in the closing kilometers. Larissa Hartog took bronze for the Netherlands.

Gomez Villafañe, representing Argentina, crossed the line sixth at 5:15 back. Tiffany Cromwell, racing in her final pro race , attacked early before finishing eighth.

Vos and Klöser pulled clear late in the race to chase the rainbow jersey.

Vos, 39, accelerated inside the final four kilometers, and Klöser fought back onto her wheel before sliding out. The Dutchwoman soloed to the line to win her career 15th world title across different disciplines.

“There was more mud than I expected. As a result, there were also some slippery sections on the course, so we had to be careful at times. Rosa was incredibly strong, especially on the climbs, where I really had to dig deep to stay with her,” Vos said.

Nannup’s punishing 125.6km course with about 3,180m of climbing is the first gravel worlds held outside Europe .

The race started after a controversial late-hour UCI decision over points that impacted dozens of riders .

Cromwell gave the locals something to cheer about when she attacked early. The favorites organized a chase behind as Cromwell opened up a gap of 1:30.

Schreurs was involved in a heavy crash with about 70km to go.

The Dutch woman lost control while riding near the front of the chasing group, went off the gravel road, and hit the ground hard.

"She has not moved." "She’s badly hit her head." 🇿🇦 Ashleigh Moolman-Pasio and 🇳🇱 Geerike Schreurs suffered heavy falls in the elite women’s race, with red flags raised following the incidents. #NannupGravel2026 | October 10-11 | SBS & SBS On Demand 📺 pic.twitter.com/mXPa1JhJBT

Moolman-Pasio, also racing her final pro race , also crashed and remained nearby as medical staff attended to the Dutch rider. There was no immediate update on possible injuries.

Vos and Klöser caught Cromwell with about 24km to go and opened up a winning gap coming into the final 10km. Klöser slipped out on a corner, and Vos drove home the victory in a wild finale.

“It was a fantastic course here in Australia. I’m really happy to have been able to secure the rainbow jersey here,” she said.

Vos now owns 15 elite world titles across four disciplines: eight in cyclocross, three on the road, two on the track and, with her win in Australia, two in gravel.

items.title: ‘I Feel Pretty Pissed Off’: UCI Under Fire for Last Minute Rule Change
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Former Australian champion Peta Mullens blasts UCI on eve of gravel worlds, saying a dozen riders unfairly affected.
items.lbText:
Peta Mullens competes in the Auscycling Cyclo-Cross National Series 2025 (Photo: Robert Cianflone/Getty Images)

Cycling’s governing body the UCI has caused controversy before with what riders and teams have said are unfair regulations. It is once more in the firing line Friday, with past Australian champion Peta Mullens accusing it of an unfair last minute rule change.

Mullens, who was Australian road race champ in 2015, expressed her frustration in a social media post. The 38 year old said she had travelled to the UCI Gravel world championships in Nannup after clear indications that she could ride the 35 to 39 year old age event.

She was all set to do so Saturday, until she and other riders were hit by unexpected news.

“I got an email from the UCI 48 hours out from the race to say that I had been bumped up to the elite field,” she said. “The reason cited was that I had 100 UCI points from the last UCI race that I competed in 14 months ago.”

Mullens qualified for the gravel worlds this summer and, conscious about having UCI points, sought to ensure there wouldn’t be an issue.

“Just to be certain I emailed them anyway [to make sure] that my UCI points weren’t a problem,” she explained. “And they replied quoting their own rulebook, which of course I had already read, and confirmed that any UCI points in a different discipline weren’t relevant to gravel. Happy days. Age group worlds, here I come.

“What happened between now and then? Well, one week ago, the UCI reversed that ruling to state that if you have any elite UCI points in any cycling discipline, you have to race elite at a world championship.”

Mullen said that she understands rules change. She said she would accept it if new regulations modified things going forward from that point. However the issue is one of timing, and the UCI backtracking on what it had previously said.

“You can’t give athletes one set of rules and let them spent thousands of dollars qualifying and travelling to a world championship,” she said. “And then change rules the week before the race, and apply it retrospectively as well.”

Mullen is clearly put out. She has incurred expenses and structured her plans around riding her age category at the worlds. It has clearly been an objective for months. However learning that she will be bumped up a level and will have to compete against current pro riders which far more experience is something she argues is wrong.

“It doesn’t just affect me,” she said. “It affects 12 other riders, half of whom have travelled from Europe. So how do I feel about it? Pretty pissed off, honestly. It feels unnecessarily unjust. Especially for a race that I was really hot to do on home soil.”

The women’s races at the gravel worlds will take place on Saturday, with the elite men’s race following on Sunday.

Mullens said efforts to negotiate appear to have had no effect.

“Myself and other athletes who are affected have been in contact with the UCI representatives who are on the ground in the last 24 hours,” she explained. “But it feels like it has all fallen on deaf ears. So tomorrow I will line up in the elite field.”

Left with no choice, she has chosen to approach that race with excitement, even if her chances of a big result have been seriously impacted.

“To the UCI, this isn’t about whether or not the rule is right or wrong,” she said.

“It is about when you chose to apply it. We play by your rules all season and then you change them at the finish line. That’s not cool.

“But also it’s not even a little bit surprising.”

items.title: Tiffany Cromwell, Ashleigh Moolman-Pasio Call It a Career at UCI Gravel Worlds after 17-Years in the Peloton
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Tiffany Cromwell and Ashleigh Moolman-Pasio have seen women's cycling completely transformed since their 2010 debut.
items.lbText:
Tiffany Cromwell pictured at the Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race with her partner, Formula One driver Valtteri Bottas (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images) (Photo: @Dario Belingheri/@Getty Images)

Two standout racers are set to hang up their wheels this weekend, ending their professional careers at the UCI Gravel Worlds in Nannup, Western Australia.

Both Tiffany Cromwell and Ashleigh Moolman-Pasio are saying goodbye after 17 seasons in the pro peloton.

They both began with the Lotto Ladies team in 2010, spending two seasons there, before branching out in different directions.

Their careers will converge one last time at the UCI Gravel Worlds this weekend in what will be an emotional weekend.

“I’ve been fortunate to have had a very long cycling career with only one major injury,” Cromwell said recently on social media. “I’ve also been able to experience and be a part of the massive change and growth of women’s cycling.

“There’s been many highs and lows and many amazing memories. And I’m happy to be able to finish on my own terms.”

The 38-year-old has had a high public profile within the sport, winning the women’s Omloop Het Nieuwsblad in 2013 plus stages of the Giro d’Italia Internazionale Femminile in 2012 and 2016.

More recently she has been dividing her time between road and gravel, winning the European championships in the latter in 2023, and also taking victories in UCI Gravel World Series races including Sea Otter Europe in 2024.

She won the Unbound Gravel 100 last year.

Over the past decade and a half she has seen huge changes in the sport, and will depart with women’s cycling in far better condition than when she started.

“I’ve been fortunate to ride this wave of women’s cycling. When we started, it was for the love of it,” the Australian told SBS. “There was limited support, the money wasn’t there. To have a career, the longevity wasn’t there.

“And then seeing the sport grow, seeing events globally pick up, seeing new disciplines like gravel come in and having the opportunity to race that and to follow the wave of gravel as well and the growth…I am very fortunate because I can appreciate where the sport has come from and where it is now, versus those coming into the sport now… They are in a lot better position but they don’t understand the demands are higher, the level is higher, the stress, everything is higher.”

Cromwell is the partner of F1 driver Valtteri Bottas, making them a pro athlete power couple of sorts.

He recently supported her at the Philadelphia Cycling Cassic, handing up bottles as the Canyon SRAM rider helped teammate Chiara Consonni to victory.

Bottas recorded a chat with Cromwell before that race, asking what her main feeling was as the end of her carer drew closer.

“I don’t have to hurt myself any more,” she said, smiling. “Except for three more times [on gravel].”

“Except when you go riding with me,” he replied.

“Then you will need to wait for me … I will need an e-bike,” she quipped.

Cromwell described the Philly event as a great one to close out the road chapter of her career. “An iconic race with so much history that was back for the first time in 10 years,” she wrote.

“The atmosphere was electric and as an added bonus we managed to take home the victory as a team with @chiara_consonnii.”

Consonnii is 11 years her junior and is one of those younger riders she said faced an environment with more opportunities than before, but also much greater demands.

Cromwell takes satisfaction in seeing this evolution take place.

“It’s been cool to watch,” she told SBS. “It is great to see that women’s cycling is finally getting to a place it deserves to be and I am sure it is going to grow in the years to come.

“I can look back and kind of talk about the old stories of what we used to have to where we are now and having the opportunity to race in races like the Tour de France avec Zwift and big gravel races, world championships, big races around the world.”

Moolman-Pasio has also competed in the biggest events and while her online exposure is less than that of the media-savvy Cromwell, she had an even bigger career.

The South African clocked up 49 wins on the road, including a Giro stage in 2021, and was second overall in the race in 2018 and 2021. GC victories include the Tour de Romandie Féminin and Emakumeen Bira.

She has been a trailblazer for African sport and will take over as general manager of Team Amani next year. The team is aiming to compete in the 2028 Tour and her experience will be invaluable in moving it towards that goal.

This weekend, though, her mind is on the worlds.

“One more time on the start line as a pro,” she wrote on Friday.

“Tomorrow is officially my last race as a professional cyclist at the Gravel World Champs in Nannup, Australia. I’d hoped to arrive feeling my best, but unfortunately I’ve come down with a head cold.

“It’s disappointing, especially because I’ve been feeling strong and I really like the course here in Nannup. But the doctor has confirmed it’s not in my chest, so I’ll be starting and seeing what the day brings. I hope to enjoy these final race kilometres and soak it all in.”

Cromwell, too, will share those sentiments. It’s a very exciting time for both, in terms of future opportunities, but also an emotional one as the final days, hours and minutes of their careers tick down.

items.title: Cycling is Cheap, $6,500 Wheels, and the Mistakes We Remember Making | Velo Podcast
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: We tally up our most memorable on-bike disasters, look at why World Tour riders are ditching BOA dials for laces, and debate the true cost of the sport.
items.lbText:
The Velo Podcast wouldn’t happen without subscribers. We’re offering listeners of the show a special 25% discount on an Outside+ membership. Enter the code velopod at checkout to score these savings, and thank you for your support!

This week, Lisa Charlebois, our host Mike Levy, and I (Josh Ross) will be riding in Death Valley when you hear this. With that in mind, we had a discussion—including Logan Jones-Wilkins who will only be on the ride in spirit—all about the mistakes we’ve made.

It starts with Logan giving me a bit of a hard time. The problem is that I’m so risk-averse I don’t actually have a ton of examples. If left to my own devices, I tend to move slowly and plan things carefully to avoid disaster. Mistakes do happen though, and I have a few. Lisa has a few more, and Logan has a few more too. Pretty soon though, this just devolves into the Levy show. Mike is far from risk-averse, and the number of things he’s done with his body moving faster than his ability to contemplate the results is pretty extensive.

We do have some other things to chat about this week before we get into all the Mike Levy disasters, though. Did you know that laces are more aerodynamic than BOA dials? Logan noticed a lot of riders at Worlds seemed to be into laces, so he jumped into why and has some interesting details to share. I also get a chance to share why I suggest that anyone looking for budget-focused shoes might want to think twice about BOA dials.

Then we take some time to answer some listener questions, including a dive into why Mike is adamant that cycling isn’t an expensive sport. That discussion is right around when we also talk about the $6,500 Partington wheels that Pidcock was riding at Worlds. Clearly, the two things are not related. Same story with the 12-speed Dura-Ace Di2 rim brake groupset that apparently still exists for sale.

As you listen, make sure you let us know your thoughts in the comments. We read them all and might discuss your thoughts on the next podcast.

items.title: Brutal Video Shows Four Cyclists Riding Over Thomas Silva’s Legs After Crash
items.author: ahood
items.content: ‘Nothing changes’: Riders vent frustration after a week of wrong-way motorcycles, vehicles on the course, and crashes that ended seasons.
items.lbText:
Thomas Silva, inset, was not seriously injured in the crash at Gran Piemonte. (Photo: Getty Images/Instagram)

Thomas Silva crashed at the final corner of Gran Piemonte on Thursday and four riders rode over him in the latest harrowing scene from a bruising week of racing in Italy .

Roadside footage captured by a fan shows the XDS-Astana rider screaming in pain as the peloton speeds past and a few even ride over his legs.

Silva was charging toward the line before he overcooked a right-hander and slammed into the fencing.

He slipped onto the asphalt and his legs were splayed into the pathway of the oncoming bunch. At least four riders struck his legs before Silva curled into the fetal position.

It’s a brutal sequence to watch. Fans frantically wave at approaching riders to slow down and steer clear, but Silva was directly in their path and there was nowhere to go for some of the ongoing riders.

Incredibly, Silva managed to stand up, get back on the bike, and finish 90th.

Team officials confirmed to Velo on Friday that the Uruguayan escaped serious injury in what was his final race of 2026.

“We had the mind and situation to end the season differently. We had a very nice season,” Silva wrote on social media. “But no complaints, thanks for the trust team!”

XDS-Astana’s Alberto Bettiol pushed on to take third behind winner Dorian Godon (Netcompany-Ineos) and Anthon Charmig (Uno-X).

Everything was coming together for Silva until the final corner.

“We were in the perfect position. Unfortunately, Thomas crashed on the final corner and wasn’t there in the final sprint,” Bettiol said. “Otherwise, I really believe we could have finished first and second. But in the end, I took third place and I’m happy with the result in the end of the season.”

For Silva, 24, it was a painful way to end a breakout season.

He won a Giro d’Italia stage and wore the maglia rosa , won back-to-back one-day wins in Spain, and a stage plus the overall at the Arctic Race of Norway.

Silva recently extended his contract through 2029, and Thursday was his last scheduled race of 2026.

Silva’s crash was the latest in a disturbing string of viral clips in a week of high-profile incidents and safety miscues across Italy.

At Monday’s Coppa Bernocchi , a DHL delivery van pulled onto the route after the breakaway passed with about 19km remaining.

Nobody crashed in that incident, and organizers later apologized.

A separate high-speed crash near the finish left Andrea Raccagni (Soudal Quick-Step) with a fractured neck vertebra. Cofidis rider Alex Aranburu fractured his collarbone and part of his pelvis.

At Tuesday’s Tre Valli Varesine, Marcel Camprubí and Thomas Gloag were involved in a collision with a police motorcycle traveling against the direction of the race .

Camprubí continued, but Gloag abandoned and needed stitches in his knee. Their Pinarello-Q36.5 captain Tom Pidcock said he was so angry he considered stopping before continuing to finish second.

“We were going 70kph on a descent and went into a round-about. We saw a motorbike coming towards us, and Thomas Gloag and me, we hit the bike,” Camprubí told Eurosport . “We are both really lucky that we were not in the hospital.

“It’s a bit frustrating, because these things happen and happen and happen, and nothing changes,” he said. “We are waiting for the facts. The team is speaking with the organization and the police, and we are still waiting for the responses.

“I think everybody can make mistakes, but when we are talking about life, we should be a bit more cautious.”

All eyes will be on Il Lombardia on Saturday, the season’s final monument and the last major race for some of the biggest stars in the elite men’s peloton.

items.title: Are Modern Bikes Too Safe? We Got a Reader Bike Build That Brings Sketchy Back.
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: We got a note from an anonymous reader of a retro-creation that blew our aero-socks off. Here are all the details of the weirdest bike we have seen all year.
items.lbText:
You ever ride gravel and think to yourself, "I wish this was harder, rougher, and more of a challenge"? One Velo reader thought so. (Photo: Trail Slayr)

We got an email the other day from a reader we couldn’t ignore. “Bikes are now better than ever—I should be so happy,” he said, “yet I wasn’t.”

Bikes are too good! Now that is a zag I would like to hear more about.

What Trayl Slayr (a Velo reader who wished to stay anonymous, only identified by this incredible pseudonym) argued was the ultimate contrarian counterpoint. Modern bikes are too stable, too fast, and too much control.

“The bike did most of the work,” Slayr said. “You just had to pedal and steer. Rider involvement and experience felt like it was waning. Over time, riding became dull.”

“So, I took back control by ‘having less control,’ if that makes sense. The idea guiding my thinking was to make a sketchy bike. Not crazy sketchy, just a bit sketchy. The ingredients I picked were a mash-up of modern goods with revived parts from 1990s mountain biking that I love.

“The results of the complete build echoed that ‘less control’ mantra in action.”

To make this slightly-sketchy gravel bike, Slayr started with a 1992 Alpinestars Cro Mega fully-rigid mountain bike. The frame is best known for its extremely elevated chainstay that ran all the way through to the middle of the downtube. The frame is steel, with True Temper OX Ultra II double-butted tubing, and has a brilliant custom powder-coated neon green-to-yellow fade finish.

So far, this tracks. Gravel is just 1990s mountain biking, right?

Nevertheless, it continued and just kept being a true beautiful mismatch. For a fork, Slayr had to go to AliExpress. Instead of a carbon fork, which most metal bikes are made with these days, the build uses a Tirus Titanium Segmented fork made for 650b wheels and cantilever brakes. This combination of a titanium fork and cantilever brakes is where much of the intentional sketchiness derives from.

“The steel elevated chainstay frame with titanium fork constantly requires my input to keep [the bike] in line,” Slayr said. “I am either rewarded or punished with lots of feedback depending on the terrain, my skill, and finesse.

“The fork flexes a bit too much, the brakes stop just enough to make me question my life choices, and keeping the cantilevers instead of doing a disc brake conversion was essential to get my ’90s muscle memory back in my hands. I instantly became smitten with this always ‘on the edge’ riding experience.”

Where the build opted for more modern trappings was in the wheel, tire, and gearing choices. Of course, with 650b wheels, modern is a relative term, but besides size, the build is much more modern than the frame and fork. Slayr has opted for a set of Kinlin XR31T 27.5/650B rims, with 32-hole count Bitex Rar12 hubs and Sapim CX-Ray spokes. All of that is a complicated way of saying the bike has durable, yet relatively lightweight 650b wheels that were paired with a set of thick, slick Ultradynamico tires.

In terms of drivetrain specs, the build uses a mix of Shimano parts and AliExpress bits to make a modified 11-speed Shimano GRX groupset. While Slayr has, ostensibly, a GRX 11-speed system that uses a 11-42 cassette, the modifications allow Slayr to use a 11-50t cassette for a much wider range of gears. According to Slayr, it is an AliExpress derailleur cage extender and oversized pulley wheels that power the system.

Throughout the bike, AliExpress is the underlying engine that brings the mismatched system together into one functional system. That only adds to the playfully sketchy attitude of this bike.

We at Velo can’t recommend this particular build. In fact, the owner doesn’t even seem to fully endorse it either, since they requested to remain anonymous. Yet, we can’t resist engaging in a build that is one-of-one in a truly unique way.

items.title: Testing 6 Completely Different Gravel Bikes Head to Head to Find the Future of Gravel
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: Gravel bikes are as varied as the people who ride them. We tested six completely different models at the Velo Field Test to find out where gravel is headed.
items.lbText:
Have you taken a look at the state of gravel cycling recently? It’s evolving faster than anyone can keep up, and so are the bikes. So we got to thinking, with the choices more varied than ever, what is the future of gravel bikes exactly? Levy, Josh, and Logan are tackling that question head on in the Velo Gravel Field Test.

For this test, we’ve assembled six models from across the entire spectrum of gravel bike design, all progressive in their own way. From a super aero bike all the way to what’s essentially a mountain bike with an identity crisis, these six bikes couldn’t be further apart from each other—oh, and that’s before we get to the one with really big wheels!

And yet they all stake a valid claim in gravel.

Beyond the consensus for needing 50mm+ of tire clearance, there’s no one approach to gravel bikes that anyone can agree on. Should they be essentially an aero road bike modified for off-roading? Should they be slack, aggressive, or somewhere in the middle? And is suspension a nebulous innovation that should stay squarely in its mountain biking lane? Don’t tell that to the brands sneaking squishy forks with various amounts of travel into gravel—we’ve got three of them in this test to parse through.

The all-rounder: race it or go adventuring.

Specification: Giant Revolt Advanced SL 0, SRAM Red XPLR Tire clearance, claimed: 53mm Weight (tested size): 17.3 pounds (ML)

Specification : Factor Sarana, SRAM Force XPLR Tire clearance, claimed : 56mm Weight (tested size) : 9.58kg (Medium)

Specification : Argon 18 Anti Matter + SRAM RED XPLR Tire clearance, claimed : 55mm Weight (tested size) : 8.5kg (Medium)

Specification : Obed GVR, SRAM Red XPLR Tire clearance, claimed : 56mm Weight (tested size) : 20.1 pounds (Medium)

Specification : Pivot Les SL Drop Bar, SRAM GX Eagle Transmission 12-Speed Tire clearance, claimed : 29 x 2.4″ Weight (tested size) : 9.78kg (Medium)

The 32er. How much difference do big wheels make?

Specification : Salsa Fargo 32 Ti, SRAM GX Eagle Transmission Tire clearance, claimed : 60mm Weight (tested size) : 20.9 pounds (Medium)

To settle the debate about the future of gravel once and for all (or perhaps muddy it more than ever), we’ve assembled three test riders who, like the bikes, couldn’t be more different.

Reformed mountain biker turned drop-bar obsessive Mike Levy leads the charge, bringing a technical, rowdy background and a preference for chunkier roads and adventuring far off the beaten path—on Earth and beyond.

He’s joined by Velo’s in-house team of tech editors. Josh Ross likes to ride long distances as efficiently as possible—catch him pedaling all day and night across the gravel roads of the Pacific Northwest and beyond. He’s all about pushing his personal boundaries, and finding the equipment that will help him go the extra mile (or extra 200 miles).

Having once finished 18th overall at the Unbound 200, Logan Jones-Wilkins can’t stop thinking about going fast and squeezing every drop of performance from gravel gear. But when he’s not mixing it up in the pointy end of races, he likes his gravel bike to be a medium for adventuring into the unknown.

That’s three different approaches to gravel, and, naturally, their takes are as varied as the riders themselves. Can they settle their differences and agree on anything? We may have to resort to some good ol’ fashioned tactics to resolve things—which may or may not mean go-kart racing.

To put these bikes to the ultimate test (and the riders too), we’ve taken everyone to the outdoor playground that is Squamish, British Columbia. Finding out the future of gravel means pushing bikes to their limits, so we’ve found a mix of terrain from single track to washboard fire roads to do just that.

We’re stress testing the bikes to get the most possible out of them. In this first episode, we’ve put together a test loop that takes our riders on a smattering of every kind of terrain one might consider gravel, from champagne roads, to loamy dirt trails, to slightly technical, rocky single track, and we’ve got climbing and descending for all of the above.

Later in the series, we take the bikes on a series of head to head timed tests including climbing, descending, and a flat road efficiency test.

To keep our testing focused on the bikes themselves, we’ve brought in control tires, 50mm Schwalbe G-One RX tires run at the same tire pressure, mounted to Easton EC90 ALX wheels .

Velo Field Test wouldn’t happen without the support of these sponsors. A big thank you to Endura for providing kits and helmets, Schwalbe for tires, and Easton for wheels!

A special thank you to the crew who made this Velo Field Test a reality!

Enjoy the video and stay tuned for episode 2 dropping next week!

items.title: ‘Helmet Saved His Life’: Dylan van Baarle Injured in Car Collision Ahead of Wedding to Ferrand-Prévot
items.author: ahood
items.content: Pauline Ferrand-Prévot describes a frightening training crash that left Dylan van Baarle needing wrist surgery ahead of their wedding.
items.lbText:
Van Baarle was involved in an incident with a motorist and his season is over. (Photo: Luc Claessen/Getty Images)

Dylan van Baarle suffered a scare just weeks ahead of his wedding to Pauline Ferrand-Prévot in an incident involving a car during a training ride Wednesday.

The Dutchman was taken to hospital after the collision in Tiel, Netherlands, according to Het Laatste Nieuws , and diagnosed with a fractured wrist.

Further details of what’s being described as a “road traffic accident involving a car” are not immediately available.

His fiancée said his helmet saved his life after a heavy impact to his head.

“He got a big impact on his head, the helmet definitely save his life,” Ferrand-Prévot wrote on Instagram . “I’m really really grateful that things turned out pretty well.”

Soudal Quick-Step confirmed that a CT scan revealed no damage to his skull or spine.

Van Baarle faces surgery Thursday and will miss Paris-Tours, ending his first season with the Belgian squad, officials confirmed.

The accident comes as one of cycling’s super couples prepares to marry later this month.

They are the only couple to have both won Paris-Roubaix : Van Baarle took his cobblestone home in 2022, and Ferrand-Prévot added hers in 2025.

Ferrand-Prévot thanked Soudal Quick-Step for arranging prompt care and friends for helping them through what she called a “really horrible, long and stressful day”.

Ferrand-Prévot — winner of the 2025 Tour de France Femmes — pulled out early in the 2026 edition and ended her season early, citing fatigue and recovery.

“I’m going to sleep alone for few nights, but that’s the tradition before the big wedding day I guess,” she wrote.

items.title: How to Watch Il Lombardia 2026 in the USA, Canada, and Worldwide
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Don't miss the final European WorldTour race of 2026 on Saturday, October 10 as Evenepoel, Seixas, Del Toro, and McNulty take on the sharp climbs of Il Lombardia.
items.lbText:
Il Lombardia will welcome a who’s who of climbing supertalents to its “race of the falling leaves” on Saturday.

Remco Evenepoel, Paul Seixas, Isaac del Toro, Tom Pidcock, Matteo Jorgenson, Primož Roglič, and newly crowned world champion Brandon McNulty headline the start list for the last European WorldTour race of the season.

The race runs a stunning 239km route from Bergamo to Como.

Expect the stacked superteams of Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe and UAE Emirates-XRG to split the haves from the have-nots in the opening procession of medium mountains.

A triple header of short climbs in the final 20km will decide the first new winner of Il Lombardia since Jakob Fuglsang in 2020.
